transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-07-19
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration approx: 52 min
Attendees: Dana Brooks (Redwood AE), Marco Lin (Redwood SE), Leah Ortiz (WyldHaven Head of Infra), Samir Patel (WyldHaven Network Eng), Nora Kim (WyldHaven Security), Evan Yu (Product)

Optional auto-summary (auto gen, may be rough):
- Goal: understand WyldHaven private deployment constraints (VPC topology, egress IP requirements, region gating, compliance).
- Key ask: whether Redwood Private can be fronted via private endpoints/peering with static egress IPs, KMS integration, and how latency/cost tradeoffs look for a mid-scale inference footprint.
- Next: share diagrams, private endpoint ranges, run pilot benchmarks.

Topics: VPC peering options, Transit Gateway vs VPC peering, PrivateLink/Private Endpoints, Egress NAT and IP whitelisting, Regional restrictions/data residency, KMS/HSM for keying, SOC2 and audit logs.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Dana: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Dana from Redwood, AE on the account. Marco our solutions engineer will walk through the networking options. Leah, do you want to start with your top constraints?
[00:23] Leah: Yeah, thanks. Uh, hi all. Our main constraints are twofold: we need all traffic to Redwood to be over our VPC or private link, no public egress for inference, and second — we need predictable egress IPs for third-party data vendors that ingest outputs. We're also under an internal policy to keep everything in eu-west and us-east for data residency.
[00:44] Marco: Got it. So private endpoints and regional pinning. We support both approaches: VPC peering/transit gateway and provider private endpoints. Side note, sometimes the wording in our docs uses PrivateLink but internally we call them private endpoints, apologies if that's mixed in speech on the call.
[01:05] Samir: Quick question — if we do peering, is there a route table hop that could affect SNAT? We need static egress for vendor whitelists, we can't maintain hundreds of IPs.
[01:20] Marco: Right. With straight VPC peering you don't get automatic static egress IPs unless you front the traffic through a NAT gateway on your side or use a managed egress appliance. Our recommended pattern for static egress is: use a dedicated egress NAT in your account — preserve one or a few elastic IPs — then route outbound inference egress through that.
[01:40] Nora: And that preserves our control and audit for outbound, right? We need logs showing file-level or request-level metadata retained for 90 days. Can Redwood ship logs into our SIEM?
[01:52] Dana: Yes, we can forward audit logs to a customer-managed SIEM endpoint; we have options for CloudWatch, Stackdriver, and direct S3 export. Note there are retention/format constraints but we can share schema.
[02:07] Evan: On latency — our product needs sub-200ms tail latency for short prompts for the chat feature. If we go private peering into a dedicated pool, do you still hit those numbers?
[02:21] Marco: Sub-200ms at tail is feasible in dedicated capacity, depends on model size and sequence length. If your prompts are short (under 64 tokens) and you pick a low-latency optimized model/quantization profile we can meet it. For hosted shared infra it's trickier during noisy neighbors. We can run a benchmark with your representative prompt set to validate.
[02:43] Leah: We also have constraint: our security team requires KMS-managed key wrapping for anything stored and for model request payload encryption at rest. How does Redwood handle customer-managed keys?
[02:58] Marco: We support customer KMS/HSM for Private deployments — integration options differ by cloud. For example, with AWS we can integrate with a customer KMS and never persist plaintext keys in our control plane. For Hosted/Shared we have limited KMS support for envelopes but not full BYOK. We'll send a doc with exact details.
[03:16] Samir: Regarding region gating — we need the inference to run only in eu-west for certain users. Can we restrict where models execute?
[03:27] Dana: Yes — our routing policies allow pinning requests to region-specific capacity. For Private deployments you can also deploy nodes only in the regions you allow. We also have fallback rules if a region is down — you can choose fail-open (route to another region) or fail-closed.
[03:42] Nora: Fail-open is not acceptable for us for regulated PII data. We'd choose fail-closed.
[03:49] Dana: Totally understood — that's a configuration on rollout. We'll note fail-closed as your default.
[04:00] Leah: Another point: we will likely want to use our own VPC endpoint with endpoint policies to lock down who can reach Redwood. Do you have sample endpoint policy configs?
[04:12] Marco: Yes, we'll attach sample endpoint policies and a sample VPC policy for the NAT approach. Also a sample Security Group layout for the private endpoints.
[04:26] Evan: Any gotchas with DNS? We use internal split-horizon DNS and don't want public lookups for Redwood endpoints.
[04:35] Marco: For private endpoints we provide a private DNS option that injects the endpoint DNS entry into your VPC resolver — so your internal name resolves to the private IP. For peering, you route by IP so DNS is up to you. Occasionally customers need to add conditional forwarders, that tends to be the trickiest part.
[04:54] Samir: About throughput: we're targeting around 120 qps peak on small requests and around 30 qps for longer contexts. Any ballpark cost or sizing guidance?
[05:06] Marco: Ballpark — for dedicated pools, you size by tokens/sec and model. I can run two scenarios: one optimized for latency (more GPUs, smaller batch size) and one optimized for cost (higher batch, less dedicated overhead). I'll produce an estimate.
[05:20] Leah: We want to avoid burst traffic going out over our NAT having unexpected charges. Is there a way Redwood limits outbound egress to our NAT quotas?
[05:34] Marco: You can set per-customer rate limiting and per-route quotas. If the client exceeds, requests get throttled with a clear 429. That helps keep egress predictable.
[05:46] Dana: Also note we can configure canary/fallback policies so if dedicated is maxed we fallback to a cheaper variant or queue requests — that's part of Redwood Optimize policies.
[05:58] Evan: About whitelisting — if vendors need to call back to an egress IP to fetch files (we hand off URLs) can we ensure those URLs are accessible from those static egress IPs only?
[06:12] Marco: Yes, if you route egress through your NAT with known EIPs, vendor whitelisting works. Alternatively, you can ask vendors to accept signed short-lived URLs to a private S3 behind a VPC endpoint.
[06:26] Leah: Ok. Can you walk us through a concrete topology diagram? Maybe walk through Transit Gateway option vs peering.
[06:36] Marco: Sure. (pauses) Option A: Direct VPC peering from WyldHaven VPC to Redwood Private VPC. Pros: simple, lower cost. Cons: managing many peering connections if you have multiple accounts/regions. Option B: Transit Gateway — one attachment to Redwood, you attach multiple WyldHaven accounts/VPCs. Pros: scalable for multi-account orgs, central egress. Cons: TGW transit costs and extra latency hop. Option C: Private endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) — a service endpoint in your VPC that maps to our NLBs. Pros: you control routing, private DNS, simple per-service access. Cons: AWS-specific, you pay per GB for PrivateLink in some cases.
[07:20] Samir: Which one gives the cleanest static egress?
[07:24] Marco: Your NAT on your side gives static egress in all patterns. TGW makes centralizing NAT easier. PrivateLink means traffic originates from your VPC, so same answer: NAT on your side.
[07:34] Nora: Audit trail: we need request-level logs for 90 days and ability to show redaction for PII. Can Redwood do selective redaction or do we have to handle redaction upstream?
[07:49] Marco: We support structured logs and can redact certain fields at ingestion; however, for strict regulatory needs we recommend doing PII redaction before sending, or use Private deployment with a customer-side preprocessor. We'll document the redaction capabilities.
[08:05] Leah: Anything specific about IPsec or extra crypto overlay for transit? We run encrypted site-to-site tunnels to our on-prem.
[08:16] Marco: You can keep your site-to-site and connect to Redwood via private endpoints inside the cloud. If you want an extra IPsec tunnel to our VPC — that is an advanced pattern; we can discuss but typically customers keep tunnel to their cloud VPC and then use peering/PrivateLink inside cloud.
[08:33] Evan: For pilot — would you recommend Hosted Private or Dedicated Reserved? We're trying to tilt to production but want to validate first.
[08:43] Dana: Pilot usually starts on Private with a small dedicated pool (reserve a few nodes). Hosted (shared) is faster but doesn't meet static egress and KMS BYOK needs. So Private/dedicated is a reasonable pilot.
[08:56] Samir: About SSO and RBAC — we'd like SCIM provisioning and SAML SSO to map system users to roles. Supported?
[09:06] Dana: Yes, we support SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning across Hosted and Private. For Private we can also integrate with your IdP inside the VPC.
[09:17] Marco: Quick note on mis-transcription: sometimes our docs refer to KV cache as K-V cash — ignore that, it's cache for context.
[09:27] (laughter)
[09:30] Leah: (laughs) good to know.
[09:33] Marco: Sorry, engineer humor.
[09:36] Nora: Compliance question: do you have any customers in finance who run Private with HSM-backed KMS?
[09:44] Dana: Yes, we have several. We'll redact exact names but share anonymized patterns and a SOC2 attestation and KMS/HSM integration guide.
[09:55] Evan: A practical question — in your private endpoint flows, what ports do we open? Is it just TLS 443?
[10:03] Marco: Primarily 443 TLS. For internal health checks we may ask for ephemeral ports between infra nodes, but those are optional in a Private deployment. We'll include a minimal security group manifest.
[10:16] Leah: We use egress filtering and DLP at the gateway. If something goes out, we want consistent prefixes to apply DLP rules. So minimizing dynamic ephemeral ports matters.
[10:28] Marco: Understood — we'll keep minimal surface area.
[10:33] Dana: Before we get too deep — any blockers to proceeding with pilot?
[10:38] Leah: Two blockers: getting exact private endpoint IP CIDRs for whitelists and approval from our security council on SOC2 docs.
[10:46] Dana: We'll provide CIDR ranges and SOC2 + KMS docs in an email.
[10:50] Samir: Also timeline — security council meets biweekly; if we can have docs this week we can move fast.
[10:58] Dana: We'll aim to send by Monday (2029-07-22).
[11:03] Marco: Noted. I'll also prepare a rough cost/throughput spreadsheet.
[11:08] Evan: One more: how does model fallback work if a particular instance is overloaded — do we risk crossing regions?
[11:18] Marco: You can set rollout to prefer same-region and fail-closed on region mismatch; or roll to another model variant in the same region. We'll make sure to configure region affinity.
[11:30] Leah: Are there any limitations on number of private endpoints we can have per account with Redwood?
[11:40] Marco: Generally limits are cloud-defined (AWS PrivateLink endpoint limits per region) — we coordinate with you to request quota increases where needed.
[11:49] Nora: Data residency: if a prompt comes from eu-west user and we route to us-east due to capacity, that is a compliance no-no. Can we enforce per-user region pinning?
[12:01] Dana: Yes, per-tenant routing policies based on request metadata can pin by geo attribute. We recommend an edge routing layer in your app to set the region header.
[12:12] Evan: Great. That answers most of product questions.
[12:16] Dana: Let's recap next steps — I'll go first. Dana to send SVG diagram of how PrivateLink and peering topologies look plus SOC2 and KMS docs and sample SG/CIDR list (by 2029-07-21). Marco to share cost/throughput estimates for two sizing scenarios and sample benchmark plan (by 2029-07-23). Leah to share VPC CIDR and architecture (by 2029-07-25). Schedule pilot week of 2029-07-29 — we'll share calendar availability.
[12:44] Leah: Sounds good. One ask — can we get a minimal runbook for incident response for the pilot? We want to know who to call and escalation steps.
[12:55] Dana: Yes, CSM will provide an SLO + runbook; I'll loop them in after this meeting.
[13:02] Samir: Small nit — when you said you can send private endpoint CIDR, do you mean we need to whitelist your entire cluster or just agent NLBs?
[13:12] Marco: We'll provide minimal NLB IP ranges (service endpoints) not whole cluster ranges. That's the doc we'll send.
[13:20] Nora: For the security council we need a one-page risk summary stating data flow and controls. Can you produce that?
[13:28] Dana: Yes, we can do a one-page architecture + control mapping to SOC2 sections.
[13:33] Evan: Anything else from WyldHaven?
[13:36] Leah: Not right now. We'll review docs and ping back.
[13:40] Dana: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and proposed pilot calendar.
[13:46] (call ends)
